domains.d: Whole-body strength: sitting, walking, running, balance
tips: Give short, frequent tummy time a few times a day.
Put toys just out of reach to encourage rolling and crawling.
Play moving games daily, like climbing over cushion hills or following a ball.
Practice stairs one step at a time, holding hands, as a game.
Turn standing on one foot and hopping into a "who lasts longest" game.
Let them run and play over an hour a day on playgrounds and tricycles.
Games that need rhythm and balance are great: catch, jump rope, bikes.
Build balance by walking along a line or making a hopping path.

domains.d: Hand and finger skills: picking up, stacking, drawing, cutting
tips: Hand them easy-to-grip rattles and cloth toys.
Let them pick up small snacks, staying close so they don't choke.
Stack blocks, put things in and out of boxes, and peel stickers together.
Let them scribble freely with chunky crayons.
Squishing clay, stringing beads and tearing paper build hand strength.
Try cutting paper strips with child scissors.
Cutting along lines, paper folding and coloring train fingertips.
Everyday games like buttoning or moving beans with chopsticks help too.

domains.d: Seeing and thinking: finding, matching, counting, comparing
tips: Play peekaboo to show how things disappear and come back.
Shake a sounding toy in different spots and let them find it.
Play "where is it?" hide-and-find and picture matching.
Join pretend play like feeding a doll.
Count "one, two, three" together when sharing snacks.
Sorting toys by size, color or shape is a great tidy-up game.
Talk about yesterday, today and tomorrow with a calendar; count with board games.
Guessing "why do you think?" together builds thinking.

domains.d: Understanding and talking: babbling, words, sentences, stories
tips: Copy their sounds, then wait and talk to them again.
Narrate your day in short words like a sportscaster.
Add one word to theirs and say it back ("water" → "water, please").
Ask names in picture books and let them point.
Answer their "why?" briefly, then ask "what do you think?"
Take time to tell today's events in order.
Play word games like word chains and riddles.
After reading, talk about characters' feelings and reasons.

domains.d: Getting along with people: eye contact, copying, turns, playing together
tips: Eye contact, smiles and talk are the best play.
Try back-and-forth games like peekaboo and pat-a-cake.
Look at what they point to and name it.
Create frequent chances to play near other kids.
Practice waiting with turn-taking games (dice, slides).
In pretend play, ask "how might the customer feel?"
Show first that it's okay to lose in rule games.
After a fight with a friend, find "what could you say?" together.

domains.d: Doing things alone: eating, dressing, washing, toileting
tips: Let them touch and pick up food at mealtimes.
While changing or dressing, ask "shall we put your arm in?"
Let them use a spoon and cup themselves, spills are okay.
Start with easy-to-remove socks and shoes.
Picture cards of the morning routine make it easier to do alone.
Practice buttoning with big-button clothes.
Build a habit of packing the next day's things together.
Praise chopstick use and washing alone generously.

fast: Does what is expected at this age well and is already trying the next step.
ok: Does most of what is expected at this age.
watch: Some skills are still shaky. Practice through play and check again in a month or two.
red: Many things expected at this age are still hard. We recommend a developmental consultation at a pediatric checkup or with a pediatrician.

rg: Have they stopped doing something they used to do?
rgEx: e.g. stopped using words they used to say, went back to crawling after walking
